insider_note: With two distinct linear factors already sitting in the denominator, this needs no A/B system of equations at all — the standard shortcut 1/[(x+a)(x+b)] = [1/(x+a) − 1/(x+b)]/(b−a) gives the split in one line.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split into partial fractions
steps.why: Writing the numerator 1 as the difference (x+2)−(x+1) — which really does equal 1 — and splitting the fraction term by term gives the two simple partial fractions directly.
common_mistakes: Setting up a full A/(x+1)+B/(x+2) system and solving for A, B, which is unnecessary extra work for two distinct linear factors this simple.
Writing 1/(x+2) − 1/(x+1) with the two terms swapped.
steps.memory_tip: (x+2)−(x+1) = 1, always — use THIS numerator trick to split two linear factors without solving equations.

steps.label: Integrate each part for the final answer
steps.why: Each partial fraction integrates to a plain log — ∫dx/(x+1) = log|x+1|, ∫dx/(x+2) = log|x+2| — and the two are subtracted, matching the split found above.
common_mistakes: Dropping the modulus bars on either log.
Combining the two logs into log|(x+1)/(x+2)| without checking that this is genuinely equal (it is, but only one form should be written, not a mix of both).
steps.memory_tip: Two logs subtracted — or equivalently, one log of the ratio (x+1)/(x+2) — either form is correct, but write only one.
